questions.q: What are the advantages of divide and conquer?
a: Better complexity: splitting often drops the running time dramatically, e.g. O(n log n) sorting instead of O(n^2).
Parallelism: the subproblems are independent of each other, so they can be solved simultaneously on multiple processors.
Simple analysis: the recurrence T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) is solved mechanically by the Master method.
Cache friendliness: working on small chunks fits better into CPU caches, which speeds up real programs noticeably.
Elegant code: the recursive structure is short and mirrors the problem definition, so it is easy to write correctly.
These advantages explain why merge sort, quick sort, binary search and Strassen's algorithm are all divide-and-conquer algorithms.

questions.q: Write the control abstraction of the divide and conquer method.
a: The control abstraction is the general recursive skeleton of divide and conquer, independent of any specific problem.
Algorithm DAndC(P)
// P is the problem instance, n its size
if Small(P) then return S(P)
else
divide P into P1, P2, ..., Pk, k >= 1
apply DAndC to each subproblem
return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk))
Small(P) tests whether P is tiny enough to solve directly; S(P) solves such a tiny instance directly.
Divide splits P into k smaller instances of the same type; each is conquered by a recursive call.
Combine merges the subproblem answers into the answer for the original problem P.
Example: in merge sort, Small(P) is true for a one-element array, and Combine is the merge step.
In short: divide, conquer recursively, combine - every divide and conquer algorithm follows this skeleton.

topics.title: Binary Search
points: Binary search finds a key in a SORTED array by repeatedly halving the search range.
It finds a key in a sorted array by repeatedly throwing away the half that cannot contain the key.
Compare key with middle element: equal means found; smaller means search left half; larger means search right half.
Pseudocode: low = 0; high = n - 1; while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2; if a[mid] == key: return mid; elif key < a[mid]: high = mid - 1; else: low = mid + 1; return -1 (not found).
Trace: search 23 in [5, 12, 23, 34, 45]. mid = index 2, a[2] = 23 = key, found immediately. Longer trace: search 34. mid = 23 < 34, so low = 3; now mid = index 3, a[3] = 34, found.
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, which solves to O(log n).
Solving it: after k steps the size is n/2^k, which reaches 1 when k = log2(n), so T(n) = O(log n). Space is O(1) for the loop version, since only a few variables are used.

The array must be sorted: the whole trick is discarding half the array after one comparison with the middle, which is valid only if everything left of the middle is smaller and everything right is larger, exactly what sorted order guarantees.

In an unsorted array the key could be hiding in the half we throw away, so the algorithm would wrongly report not found. Therefore sorting is a precondition, not an optimisation: sort once at O(n log n) and then enjoy O(log n) searches forever after.
Halving the problem at every step is what makes binary search exponentially faster than a linear scan.

questions.q: Explain binary search with an example. What is its time complexity?
a: Binary search finds a key in a SORTED array by repeatedly throwing away the half that cannot contain the key.
Pseudocode:
low = 0; high = n - 1
while low <= high:
mid = (low + high) // 2
if a[mid] == key: return mid
elif key < a[mid]: high = mid - 1
else: low = mid + 1
return -1 # not found
Trace: search 23 in [5, 12, 23, 34, 45]. mid = index 2, a[2] = 23 = key, found immediately.
Longer trace: search 34. mid = 23 < 34, so low = 3; now mid = index 3, a[3] = 34, found.
Each comparison halves the search range, giving the recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + 1.
Solving it: after k steps the size is n/2^k, which reaches 1 when k = log2(n), so T(n) = O(log n).
Space is O(1) for the loop version, since only a few variables are used.
Halving the problem at every step is what makes binary search exponentially faster than a linear scan.

questions.q: Why must the array be sorted for binary search?
a: The whole trick of binary search is discarding half the array after a single comparison with the middle element.
That decision is valid only if everything left of the middle is smaller and everything right is larger - which is exactly what sorted order guarantees.
In an unsorted array the key could be hiding in the half we throw away, so the algorithm would wrongly report not found.
Therefore sorting is a precondition, not an optimisation: we sort once at O(n log n) and then enjoy O(log n) searches forever after.
Sorted order is the logical foundation the halving argument stands on; without it the algorithm is simply incorrect.

topics.title: Finding Maximum and Minimum
points: Straightforward method: scan once, 2n - 2 comparisons in the worst case.

The straightforward method finds the maximum and the minimum in two separate scans: first scan compares each new element with the current maximum (n - 1 comparisons), second scan compares with the current minimum (another n - 1). Total: (n - 1) + (n - 1) = 2n - 2.
Example: for n = 100 numbers, that is 198 comparisons. It is simple to write but wasteful, because every element is compared twice.
Divide and conquer: split array, find max/min of each half, compare the two results.
D&C needs only about 3n/2 - 2 comparisons, better than 2n - 2.

D&C idea: instead of comparing every element against the running max and min, first pair elements up and compare them with each other. Divide the array into two halves; recursively find (max1, min1) of the left half and (max2, min2) of the right half; then overall max = larger of max1 and max2 (1 comparison) and overall min = smaller of min1 and min2 (1 comparison).
Combining two halves costs only 2 comparisons, giving the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2, which solves to about 3n/2 - 2 comparisons.
Example: for n = 100, divide and conquer needs about 148 comparisons versus 198 for the naive method. The saving comes from letting elements eliminate each other before facing the current champions.

Worked comparison for n = 6: linear search needs 2 comparisons per element after the first, so 2n - 2 = 10 comparisons. Divide and conquer (pair method): pair up the 6 elements (3 comparisons) to get 3 pair-winners and 3 pair-losers; find the max of the 3 winners (2 comparisons); find the min of the 3 losers (2 comparisons). Total = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 comparisons, 3 fewer for the same answer.

questions.q: How many comparisons does the straightforward max-min algorithm need?
a: The straightforward method finds the maximum and the minimum in two separate scans of the array.
First scan: compare each new element with the current maximum - that takes n - 1 comparisons.
Second scan: compare each new element with the current minimum - another n - 1 comparisons.
Total in the worst case: (n - 1) + (n - 1) = 2n - 2 comparisons.
Example: for n = 100 numbers, that is 198 comparisons.
It is simple to write but wasteful, because every element is compared twice - once against the max and once against the min.
The divide-and-conquer version below cuts this to about 3n/2 - 2 by comparing elements with each other first.

questions.q: Explain the divide and conquer approach for max and min.
a: Idea: instead of comparing every element against the running max and min, first pair elements up and compare them with each other.
Divide the array into two halves; recursively find (max1, min1) of the left half and (max2, min2) of the right half.
overall max = larger of max1 and max2 # 1 comparison
overall min = smaller of min1 and min2 # 1 comparison
Combining two halves costs only 2 comparisons, giving the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2.
This solves to about 3n/2 - 2 comparisons, clearly better than the straightforward 2n - 2.
Example: for n = 100, divide and conquer needs about 148 comparisons versus 198 for the naive method.
The saving comes from letting elements eliminate each other before facing the current champions.

questions.q: For an array of 6 elements, compare the number of comparisons needed to find both the maximum and minimum using linear search and divide and conquer.
a: Linear search (straightforward method): compare each new element with the current max and the current min - 2 comparisons per element after the first.
Comparisons = 2n - 2 = 2(6) - 2 = 10 comparisons.
Divide and conquer (pair method): pair up the 6 elements - 3 comparisons produce 3 pair-winners and 3 pair-losers.
Find the max of the 3 winners: 2 comparisons. Find the min of the 3 losers: 2 comparisons.
Total = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 comparisons.
So divide and conquer needs 7 comparisons against 10 for linear search - 3 fewer for the same answer.
Answer: linear search 10 comparisons, divide and conquer 7 comparisons.

topics.title: Merge Sort
points: Divide the array into halves, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves.

Pseudocode: mergesort(a): if len(a) <= 1: return a; mid = len(a) // 2; left = mergesort(a[:mid]); right = mergesort(a[mid:]); return merge(left, right), where merge is a linear scan taking the smaller front element.
Trace on [38, 27, 43, 3]: split into [38, 27] and [43, 3], which sort to [27, 38] and [3, 43]. Merge: compare 27 vs 3, take 3; 27 vs 43, take 27; 38 vs 43, take 38; then 43. Result: [3, 27, 38, 43].
Merge step is linear: compare front elements and take the smaller, O(n).
Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives O(n log n) in best, average AND worst case.

Why O(n log n) even in the worst case: the split always cuts the array into two exactly equal halves, so the recursion depth is always log2(n) and no input can change it. At every level the merge scans all n elements once, so total work = n x log n for every input without exception.
Contrast quick sort: its split depends on the pivot, so a bad pivot gives an unbalanced tree and O(n^2). Merge sort's balanced partition is built in.

Recursion tree for 10 elements, [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10, 5, 21, 16]: level 0 has all 10; level 1 has two nodes of 5; level 2 has four nodes of sizes 3, 2, 3, 2; level 3 splits further; level 4 has ten single-element leaves (the base case). Merging climbs back up: every level merges n elements, and there are ceil(log2 10) = 4 levels, so total work is O(n log n).
Stable sort, but needs O(n) extra space; not in-place. Space cost is O(n) extra for the merge buffers.

Drawbacks: extra memory (quick sort and heap sort work in place); recursion overhead (for tiny subarrays the call cost exceeds the sorting work); not adaptive (full n log n work even on an already sorted array, unlike insertion sort's O(n) best case).

In practice libraries fix this with a hybrid: use merge sort down to small sizes, then finish with insertion sort. So merge sort trades memory for a rock-solid time guarantee, the right call when memory is available.

questions.q: Explain merge sort with an example and analyse its complexity.
a: Merge sort is the classic divide-and-conquer sort: split the array into halves, sort each half recursively, then merge the sorted halves.
Pseudocode:
mergesort(a):
if len(a) <= 1: return a
mid = len(a) // 2
left = mergesort(a[:mid]); right = mergesort(a[mid:])
return merge(left, right) # linear scan taking the smaller front element
Trace on [38, 27, 43, 3]: split into [38, 27] and [43, 3]; these sort to [27, 38] and [3, 43].
Merge step: compare 27 vs 3, take 3; 27 vs 43, take 27; 38 vs 43, take 38; then 43.
Recurrence: two halves plus a linear merge gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which solves to O(n log n).
Because the split is always exactly half, this bound holds for the best, average AND worst case alike.
Space cost: O(n) extra for the merge buffers.
Merge sort is also stable: equal elements keep their original relative order.
Guaranteed O(n log n) in every case is why merge sort is the safe choice for sorting.

questions.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n) even in the worst case?
a: The split step always cuts the array into two exactly equal halves, no matter what the data looks like.
So the recursion depth is always log2(n); no input can make the tree deeper or shallower.
At every level, the merge step scans all n elements once across the subproblems, doing n total work per level.
Total work = (work per level) x (number of levels) = n x log n, for every possible input without exception.
Contrast quick sort: its split depends on the pivot, so a bad pivot gives an unbalanced tree and O(n^2).
Merge sort's perfectly balanced partition is built into the algorithm, so the worst case cannot escape O(n log n).

questions.q: What are the drawbacks of merge sort?
a: Extra memory: merging needs O(n) auxiliary space, while quick sort and heap sort work in place.
Recursion overhead: for tiny subarrays the function-call cost exceeds the sorting work, making it slower than insertion sort there.
Not adaptive: it does the full n log n work even on an already sorted array, unlike insertion sort's O(n) best case.
In practice libraries fix this with a hybrid: use merge sort down to small sizes, then finish with insertion sort.
So merge sort trades memory for a rock-solid time guarantee - the right call when memory is available.

questions.q: Illustrate the recursion tree of merge sort for 10 elements.
a: The recursion tree of merge sort shows how the array keeps splitting until single elements, then merges back up.
Level 0: one node holding all 10 elements.
Level 4: ten single-element leaves - the base case, each already sorted.
Merging climbs back up: every level merges n elements in total, and there are ceil(log2 10) = 4 levels, so the total work is O(n log n).
In short: the tree has 4 levels above the leaves and shows exactly why merge sort costs O(n log n).

topics.title: Quick Sort
points: Pick a pivot, PARTITION so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then sort both sides recursively.
Quick sort picks one element as the pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then sorts both sides recursively.
Lomuto partition pseudocode: pivot = a[low]; i = low; for j in range(low+1, high+1): if a[j] < pivot: i += 1; swap(a[i], a[j]); swap(a[low], a[i]) (pivot into its final position); return i.
Trace on [10, 7, 8, 9, 1, 5] with pivot 10: every smaller element is swept left, giving [7, 8, 9, 1, 5, 10]. The pivot 10 is now fixed at the end and never moves again; recurse on [7, 8, 9, 1, 5].
Each partition scans its segment once, costing O(n) for the combine step of that level. Since every element becomes a pivot exactly once, each is placed into its final position exactly once.
Partitioning is the heart of quick sort; everything else is just recursion on the two sides.
Best and average case: pivot splits evenly, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = O(n log n).
Worst case: pivot is always smallest or largest (e.g. sorted array, first element as pivot), T(n) = T(n-1) + n = O(n^2).

The behaviour depends entirely on where the pivot lands: best case, the pivot always lands in the middle (recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which solves to O(n log n)); worst case, the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, so one side is empty and the other holds n-1 elements (recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + n = n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = O(n^2)).

This worst case strikes with an already sorted array when the first element is always chosen as pivot. The average case over random inputs is O(n log n), which is why quick sort is fast in practice despite the bad worst case. In short: balanced pivots give n log n, degenerate pivots give n^2; pivot choice is everything.
In-place and fast in practice; not stable.

Merge sort vs quick sort: both are divide-and-conquer sorts with O(n log n) average time, but they differ in guarantees and resources. Time: merge sort is O(n log n) in best, average and worst case; quick sort is O(n log n) on average but O(n^2) in the worst case. Space: merge sort needs O(n) extra memory for merging; quick sort sorts in place using only O(log n) recursion stack. Stability: merge sort is stable (equal elements keep their order); quick sort's swapping makes it unstable. Practical speed: quick sort usually wins because of smaller constants and better cache behaviour from in-place access.

Choice rule: need a guaranteed time bound or stability, choose merge sort; need speed and low memory, choose quick sort. This comparison is a favourite exam question because it tests the whole divide-and-conquer chapter at once.

Avoiding the worst case: the worst case comes from bad pivots, so choose pivots that are unlikely to be extreme. Random pivot: pick the pivot randomly instead of always the first element; an adversary cannot then feed a killer input, and the expected time stays O(n log n). Median-of-three: take the median of the first, middle and last elements as the pivot; this kills the sorted-input worst case completely. Hybrid approach: switch to insertion sort for tiny subarrays (e.g. below 10 elements) to cut recursion overhead. Introspective sort, used in the C++ STL, watches the recursion depth and switches to heap sort if it grows too deep, guaranteeing O(n log n). With a decent pivot rule, the O(n^2) case becomes a theoretical curiosity rather than a practical danger.

Lomuto partition pseudocode:

for j in range(low+1, high+1):
if a[j] < pivot: i += 1; swap(a[i], a[j])

Since every element becomes a pivot exactly once, each is placed into its final position exactly once.
Partitioning is the heart of quick sort - everything else is just recursion on the two sides.

a: The behaviour of quick sort depends entirely on where the pivot lands after partitioning.

Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n (partitioning costs n), which solves to O(n
log n).
Worst case: the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, so one side is empty and the other holds n-1 elements.

questions.q: Compare merge sort and quick sort.
a: Both are divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms with O(n log n) average time, but they differ in guarantees and resources.
Time: merge sort is O(n log n) in best, average and worst case; quick sort is O(n log n) on average but O(n^2) in the worst case.
Space: merge sort needs O(n) extra memory for merging; quick sort sorts in place using only O(log n) recursion stack.

Choice rule: need a guaranteed time bound or stability - merge sort; need speed and low memory - quick sort.
This comparison is a favourite exam question because it tests the whole divide-and-conquer chapter at once.

questions.q: How can the quick sort worst case be avoided?
a: The worst case comes from bad pivots, so the fix is to choose pivots that are unlikely to be extreme.
Random pivot: pick the pivot randomly instead of always the first element; an adversary cannot then feed a killer input, and the expected time stays O(n log n).
Median-of-three: take the median of the first, middle and last elements as the pivot; this kills the sorted-input worst case completely.
Hybrid approach: switch to insertion sort for tiny subarrays (e.g. below 10 elements) to cut recursion overhead.
Introspective sort, used in the C++ STL, goes further: it watches the recursion depth and switches to heap sort if it grows too deep, guaranteeing O(n log n).
With a decent pivot rule, the O(n^2) case becomes a theoretical curiosity rather than a practical danger.

topics.title: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication
points: Normal multiplication of two n x n matrices needs 8 half-size multiplications: O(n^3).
Strassen uses 7 clever multiplications (M1 to M7) plus additions, trading 1 multiplication for extra additions.

Strassen's insight: with clever additions and subtractions of the submatrices, only 7 multiplications are enough to build all four result blocks. One expensive multiplication is traded for several cheap additions, and multiplication dominates the cost.
Recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2), giving O(n^log2(7)) = O(n^2.81), better than n^3.
Recurrence detail: 7 subproblems of size n/2 plus O(n^2) additions and subtractions to combine them, with T(1) = O(1).

Solve by the Master method: a = 7, b = 2, f(n) = n^2. Compare n^(log2 7) = n^2.81 against f(n) = n^2; since n^2.81 grows polynomially faster, this is Master case 1, where the subproblems dominate the cost.
Therefore T(n) = Theta(n^(log2 7)) = Theta(n^2.81). The exponent drops from 3 to 2.81 purely because 7 multiplications replaced 8.
Example: for n = 1024, n^3 is about 10^9 operations while n^2.81 is roughly 3 x 10^8, a 3x saving.
Strassen proved that matrix multiplication is fundamentally easier than cubic, opening the whole field of fast matrix algorithms.

Limitations: high constant factors from the many additions, subtractions and bookkeeping; a crossover point, it beats naive O(n^3) only for large matrices, typically n above a few hundred; extra memory for the intermediate sum and difference matrices; numerical stability, more additions mean more rounding-error accumulation in floating point; and implementation complexity, far harder to write and debug than three nested loops.
So Strassen is a theoretical breakthrough that libraries use selectively, not a drop-in replacement for everyday multiplication.
Best for large matrices; overhead makes it slower for small ones.

questions.q: Explain Strassen's matrix multiplication. Why is it faster?
a: Standard matrix multiplication of two n x n matrices needs O(n^3) operations; a plain divide-and-conquer version needs 8 half-size multiplications.
Strassen's insight: with clever additions and subtractions of the submatrices, only 7 multiplications (M1 to M7) are enough to build all four result blocks.
One expensive multiplication is traded for several cheap additions, and multiplication dominates the cost.
Recurrence: 7 subproblems of size n/2 plus O(n^2) additions gives T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2).
By the Master method this solves to O(n^2.81), since log2(7) is about 2.81, which beats n^3 for large n.
Example: for n = 1024, n^3 is about 10^9 operations while n^2.81 is roughly 3 x 10^8 - a 3x saving.
Strassen proved that matrix multiplication is fundamentally easier than cubic, opening the whole field of fast matrix algorithms.

questions.q: Write the recurrence for Strassen's algorithm and solve it.
a: At each level Strassen creates 7 subproblems of half the size and does O(n^2) additions and subtractions to combine them.
Recurrence: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + c*n^2, with T(1) = O(1).
Apply the Master method: a = 7, b = 2, f(n) = n^2.
Compare n^(log_b a) = n^(log2 7) = n^2.81 against f(n) = n^2.
Since n^2.81 grows polynomially faster than n^2, we are in Master case 1: the subproblems dominate the cost.
Therefore T(n) = Theta(n^(log2 7)) = Theta(n^2.81).
The exponent drops from 3 to 2.81 purely because 7 multiplications replaced 8.

questions.q: What are the limitations of Strassen's algorithm?
a: High constant factors: the many additions, subtractions and complex bookkeeping make each recursion level expensive.
Crossover point: it only beats the naive O(n^3) method for large matrices, typically n above a few hundred.
Extra memory: the intermediate sum and difference matrices need additional storage beyond the inputs.
Numerical stability: more additions mean more rounding-error accumulation in floating-point arithmetic.
Implementation complexity: the code is far harder to write and debug than three nested loops.
So Strassen is a theoretical breakthrough that libraries use selectively, not a drop-in replacement for everyday multiplication.

topics.title: Greedy Method: General Concept
points: Greedy builds the answer step by step, always picking the locally best choice, never reconsidering.
The greedy strategy builds an answer step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never reconsidering earlier choices. Greedy is take the best now, never look back.
Works only when local optimum leads to global optimum (greedy-choice property plus optimal substructure).

It only works for problems with two structural properties. Greedy-choice property: a globally optimal answer can be assembled from locally optimal choices, meaning the first greedy pick is always part of some optimum. Optimal substructure: after making the greedy choice, the remaining problem is a smaller copy of the original.
Example where it works: coin change with coins 25, 10, 5, 1; repeatedly taking the largest coin that fits always uses the fewest coins.
Examples: fractional knapsack, Prim's, Kruskal's, Dijkstra's, Huffman coding.

Feasible vs optimal solution: a feasible solution is any candidate answer that satisfies all the constraints of the problem, whether or not it is the best one. An optimal solution is the feasible solution with the best objective value, maximum profit or minimum cost.

Example: knapsack with capacity 10, item A (weight 6, profit 12) and item B (weight 5, profit 9). Picking only A is feasible (weight 6 <= 10) with profit 12; picking only B is feasible with profit 9; picking A + B together is not feasible (weight 11 > 10). The optimal solution is picking A alone, profit 12, the best among all feasible picks. In short: feasible means allowed, optimal means allowed and best.
Fails on 0/1 knapsack: a greedy pick can block the true optimum.

The classic failure: items A (profit 60, weight 10), B (100, 20), C (120, 30); capacity 50. Greedy by profit-to-weight ratio picks A first (ratio 6), then B (ratio 5): total weight 30, profit 160, and C no longer fits. The true optimum takes B and C: weight 50, profit 220, which greedy never finds because it committed to A.

The failure happens because the greedy-choice property is missing: the locally best item A is not part of the global optimum. Note the contrast: fractional knapsack allows taking part of C, and there greedy is optimal. This example is the standard exam proof that greedy needs the right problem structure.

Control abstraction, the general skeleton every greedy algorithm follows: Algorithm Greedy(a, n) // a[1:n] holds the n inputs: solution = empty; for i = 1 to n do: x = Select(a); if Feasible(solution, x) then solution = Union(solution, x); return solution.

Select(a) picks the remaining input that looks best by the greedy criterion, e.g. the highest profit per weight. Feasible(solution, x) checks that adding x keeps a valid partial answer, e.g. the total weight stays within capacity. Union(solution, x) adds x to the answer; a greedy choice is never reconsidered later.

Example: fractional knapsack: Select picks the highest-ratio item, Feasible checks the capacity, Union adds it or a fraction of it. In short: repeatedly select the best-looking feasible input; simple and fast, but correct only when the greedy-choice property holds.

Subset paradigm: greedy problems fall into two paradigms. Subset paradigm: the answer is a subset of the n inputs, we decide for each input whether to take it or not; examples are knapsack (which items to pack), Prim's and Kruskal's (which edges form the minimum spanning tree). Ordering paradigm: the answer is an ordering of the inputs, e.g. scheduling jobs in some sequence.

All the greedy problems in this syllabus, knapsack, Prim's, Kruskal's, Dijkstra's, are subset paradigm: each step picks one more input into the solution set. In short: in the subset paradigm the answer is built as a set of chosen inputs.

questions.q: Explain the greedy strategy. When does it work?
a: The greedy strategy builds an answer step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never reconsidering earlier choices.
It is simple and fast, but it only works for problems with two structural properties.
Greedy-choice property: a globally optimal answer can be assembled from locally optimal choices - the first greedy pick is always part of some optimum.
Optimal substructure: after making the greedy choice, the remaining problem is a smaller copy of the original.
Example where it works: coin change with coins 25, 10, 5, 1 - repeatedly taking the largest coin that fits always uses the fewest coins.
Syllabus examples that are all greedy: fractional knapsack, Prim's, Kruskal's and Dijkstra's algorithms.
Greedy is take the best now, never look back - correct only when the problem's structure forgives short-sightedness.

topics.title: Knapsack Problem
points: Knapsack: n items with profit p and weight w, capacity M; maximise profit without exceeding M.
Fractional knapsack: items can be split; greedy by profit/weight ratio is optimal, O(n log n).
0/1 knapsack: items taken whole or not at all; greedy fails, needs dynamic programming.

Fractional knapsack greedy steps: step 1, compute the profit-to-weight ratio p/w for every item; step 2, sort items by ratio in descending order, costing O(n log n); step 3, walk down the sorted list, taking each whole item if it fits, otherwise taking exactly the fraction that fills the knapsack, then stop.

Worked example: M = 50; items A (60, 10), B (100, 20), C (120, 30); ratios 6, 5, 4. Take all of A: weight 10, profit 60; remaining 40. Take all of B: weight 20, profit 100; remaining 20. Take 20/30 of C: profit (20/30)*120 = 80. Knapsack full. Total profit = 60 + 100 + 80 = 240, and this is provably optimal.
Optimality argument: any optimum can be rearranged to take items in ratio order without losing profit, so greedy matches it. Complexity: O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) for the scan.
Divisibility is what makes the greedy choice safe here, unlike the 0/1 version.

Fractional vs 0/1 knapsack: the difference is divisibility. Fractional: the greedy algorithm sorting by profit-to-weight ratio is optimal, running in O(n log n). 0/1: greedy can fail, so dynamic programming over capacity is needed, costing O(n*M). Fractional is solvable in polynomial time; 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard in general.

Example: with capacity 50 and items (60,10), (100,20), (120,30), fractional gives 240 while 0/1 gives 220 by a different choice. Memory aid: fractional means greedy works; zero-one means DP is needed. One word, divisible or not, decides the entire algorithm.

Worked example: weights (10, 20, 30, 25, 28), profits (60, 100, 120, 75, 140), capacity 50. Ratios: 60/10 = 6.0, 100/20 = 5.0, 120/30 = 4.0, 75/25 = 3.0, 140/28 = 5.0. Sorted descending: Item 1 (6.0), Item 2 (5.0), Item 5 (5.0), Item 3 (4.0), Item 4 (3.0). Take Item 1 fully: weight 10, profit 60, remaining 40. Take Item 2 fully: weight 20, profit 100, remaining 20. Item 5 weighs 28 but only 20 fits: take the fraction 20/28, profit 140 x 20/28 = 100, remaining 0. Total profit = 60 + 100 + 100 = 260.

questions.q: Solve fractional knapsack with the greedy method. Give steps.
a: In the fractional knapsack, items may be split, and the goal is maximum profit within capacity M.
Step 1: compute the profit-to-weight ratio p/w for every item.
Step 2: sort items by ratio in descending order - this costs O(n log n).
Step 3: walk down the sorted list; take each whole item if it fits, otherwise take exactly the fraction that fills the knapsack, then stop.
Worked example: M = 50; items A (60, 10), B (100, 20), C (120, 30); ratios 6, 5, 4.
Take all of A: weight 10, profit 60. Remaining capacity 40.
Take all of B: weight 20, profit 100. Remaining capacity 20.
Take 20/30 of C: profit (20/30)*120 = 80. Knapsack full.
Total profit = 60 + 100 + 80 = 240, and this is provably optimal.
Optimality argument: any optimum can be rearranged to take items in ratio order without losing profit, so greedy matches it.
Complexity: O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) for the scan.
Divisibility is what makes the greedy choice safe here, unlike the 0/1 version.

topics.title: Prim's Algorithm
points: Prim's finds the Minimum Spanning Tree: cheapest set of edges connecting all vertices, no cycles.
Grow one tree: start anywhere, repeatedly add the cheapest edge joining the tree to an outside vertex.
Uses a greedy choice; with a simple array it is O(V^2), with a heap O(E log V).

questions.q: Explain Prim's algorithm step by step with an example.
a: Prim's algorithm finds the Minimum Spanning Tree: the cheapest set of edges connecting all vertices without forming cycles.
It grows a single tree, starting from any vertex, always attaching the cheapest edge that reaches outside the tree.
Pseudocode:
tree = {start}; repeat V-1 times:
pick the minimum-weight edge (u, v) with u in tree, v outside
add v and the edge to the tree
Trace on triangle A-B 1, B-C 2, A-C 3, starting at A.
Tree = {A}. Edges from the tree outward: A-B (1), A-C (3). Pick A-B.
Tree = {A, B}. Edges outward: A-C (3), B-C (2). Pick B-C.
Tree = {A, B, C}. Done. MST edges: A-B, B-C with total cost 3.
Note A-C (3) was never taken: it would close the cycle A-B-C-A.
Complexity: O(V^2) with a simple array scanning for the minimum; O(E log V) with a min-heap.
The greedy choice is safe by the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST.
Prim's is Dijkstra-like growth, but minimising edge weight instead of distance from the source.
tags: SURE MARK (May 2019, Oct 2021, Feb 2025, Oct 2025 H)

questions.q: Why does the greedy choice work in Prim's algorithm?
a: The justification is the cut property of minimum spanning trees.
Cut property: for any partition of the vertices into two sets, the lightest edge crossing between them belongs to at least one MST.

Proof sketch: if some MST avoided that lightest edge, adding it creates a cycle; removing the heaviest edge of that cycle gives another spanning tree that is no costlier - so the lightest edge is safe.
At every step, Prim's current tree defines exactly such a cut: vertices inside the tree versus outside.
The algorithm picks the lightest edge crossing this cut, which the property guarantees is safe to include.
Since every added edge is safe, the finished tree of V-1 edges must be a minimum spanning tree.
The cut property is the one-line proof that Prim's greedy choices never go wrong.
tags: SURE MARK (May 2019, Oct 2021, Feb 2025, Oct 2025 H)

topics.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
points: Kruskal's also finds the MST: sort ALL edges by weight, add the cheapest one that does not form a cycle.
Kruskal's finds the MST by considering all edges globally, cheapest first, skipping any edge that would form a cycle.
Cycle check uses disjoint sets (union-find): skip an edge if its ends are already connected.

Pseudocode: sort all edges by weight ascending; make a separate set for each vertex; for each edge (u, v) in sorted order: if find(u) != find(v): add edge to MST and union(u, v); else skip it (it would create a cycle).

Trace on edges AB 1, BC 2, AC 3. Sorted: AB(1), BC(2), AC(3). Take AB: sets become {A,B}, {C}. Take BC: find(B) != find(C), so merge into {A,B,C}; MST so far: AB, BC. AC: find(A) == find(C), both in {A,B,C}, so skip it, it would close a cycle. MST cost = 1 + 2 = 3.
Cycle detection uses disjoint-set union (union-find), nearly O(1) per operation with path compression and union by rank.
Complexity dominated by sorting: O(E log E).
Prim's vs Kruskal's: both are greedy algorithms that produce a minimum spanning tree of the same minimum total cost.
Growth style: Prim's grows a single tree outward from a start vertex; Kruskal's merges a forest by scanning a globally sorted edge list.
Data needed: Prim's works from the adjacency structure of the graph; Kruskal's works naturally from a plain edge list.

Complexity: Prim's is O(V^2) in the simple version or O(E log V) with a heap; Kruskal's is O(E log E), dominated by sorting. Dense graphs (many edges): Prim's O(V^2) wins. Sparse graphs (few edges): Kruskal's O(E log E) wins.
Implementation: Prim's needs a priority queue of frontier vertices; Kruskal's needs union-find for cycle checks.
Memory aid: Prim grows, Kruskal sorts. Same answer, different strategy: pick based on how dense the graph is.

questions.q: Explain Kruskal's algorithm step by step with an example.
a: Kruskal's finds the MST by considering all edges globally, cheapest first, skipping any edge that would form a cycle.
Pseudocode:
sort all edges by weight ascending
make a separate set for each vertex
for each edge (u, v) in sorted order:
if find(u) != find(v): add edge to MST; union(u, v)
else: skip it # would create a cycle
Trace on edges AB 1, BC 2, AC 3.
Sorted: AB(1), BC(2), AC(3). Take AB: sets become {A,B}, {C}.
Take BC: find(B) != find(C), so merge into {A,B,C}. MST so far: AB, BC.
AC: find(A) == find(C), both in {A,B,C} - skip, it would close a cycle.
MST cost = 1 + 2 = 3.
Cycle detection uses disjoint-set union (union-find), nearly O(1) per operation with path compression and union by rank.
Complexity is dominated by sorting: O(E log E).
Sort globally, take greedily, skip cycles - that is the whole algorithm.

questions.q: Compare Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.
a: Both are greedy algorithms that produce a minimum spanning tree of the same minimum total cost.
Growth style: Prim's grows a single tree outward from a start vertex; Kruskal's merges a forest by scanning a globally sorted edge list.
Data needed: Prim's works from the adjacency structure of the graph; Kruskal's works naturally from a plain edge list.
Complexity: Prim's is O(V^2) in the simple version or O(E log V) with a heap; Kruskal's is O(E log E), dominated by sorting.
Dense graphs (many edges): Prim's O(V^2) wins.
Sparse graphs (few edges): Kruskal's O(E log E) wins.
Implementation: Prim's needs a priority queue of frontier vertices; Kruskal's needs union-find for cycle checks.
Memory aid: Prim grows, Kruskal sorts.
Same answer, different strategy - pick based on how dense the graph is.

topics.title: Dijkstra's Single Source Shortest Path
points: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source to all vertices in a graph with non-negative weights.
Greedy: keep dist[] (best known distance); repeatedly finalise the unsettled vertex with smallest dist and relax its edges.
Relaxation: if dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v], update dist[v].
O(V^2) simple, O(E log V) with heap; FAILS with negative edge weights.

questions.q: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm step by step with an example.
a: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source to all vertices, requiring non-negative edge weights.
It maintains dist[], the best known distance to each vertex, and repeatedly finalises the closest unsettled vertex.
Pseudocode:
dist[source] = 0; dist[others] = infinity; settled = empty
repeat V times:
u = unsettled vertex with smallest dist; mark u settled
for each neighbour v of u: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u,v)) #
relaxation
Trace: edges S-A 4, S-B 2, B-A 1.
Start: dist = {S:0, A:inf, B:inf}.
Settle S (0): relax neighbours -> A = 4, B = 2.
Settle B (2): relax A -> min(4, 2+1) = 3.
Settle A (3). Final distances: S = 0, B = 2, A = 3. The path S-B-A (2+1)
beats the direct S-A (4).
Complexity: O(V^2) with a simple array; O(E log V) with a min-heap, since each edge is relaxed once.
Correctness idea: the unsettled vertex with smallest dist cannot be improved later, because all weights are non-negative.
Dijkstra is the standard single-source shortest path algorithm wherever weights are non-negative.

questions.q: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail with negative weights?
a: Dijkstra's core promise is: once a vertex is settled, its distance is final and will never improve.
That promise holds only because non-negative weights mean any alternative route through unsettled vertices can only be longer.
A negative edge breaks it: a shorter path to an already settled vertex can appear later via that edge.
Example: S-A weight 5, S-B weight 3, B-A weight -4.
Dijkstra settles A at 5, then discovers S-B-A = -1, but A is already closed.
The true shortest distance to A is -1, which Dijkstra misses - the answer is wrong, not just slow.
Fix: use Bellman-Ford, which relaxes all edges V-1 times and handles negative weights correctly (though not negative cycles).
Settled means final is true only when no edge can pull a distance down afterwards.

questions.q: What is edge relaxation?
a: Relaxation is the single operation at the heart of Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd Warshall.
It asks: is the path to v better when routed through u?
if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w(u, v)
In words: if going source -> ... -> u -> v beats the current best distance to v, update it.
Repeated relaxation propagates improvements outward until no distance can shrink further.
Example: dist[A] = 4, and edge B-A has weight 1 with dist[B] = 2.
Since 2 + 1 = 3 < 4, dist[A] becomes 3.
Every shortest-path algorithm is just relaxation applied in a clever order.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming: General Concept
points: DP solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by solving each subproblem once and storing the answer.
Two styles: memoization (top-down recursion plus cache) and tabulation (bottom-up table).
Classic example: Fibonacci.
Naive recursion is O(2^n); DP makes it O(n).
Steps: define subproblems, write recurrence, compute bottom-up (or memoized), read answer.

questions.q: Explain dynamic programming. How is it different from divide and conquer?
a: Dynamic programming solves problems whose subproblems overlap: each distinct subproblem is solved once, stored, and reused instead of being recomputed.
It needs two properties: overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure (an optimum built from optima of subproblems).
Classic example: Fibonacci. fib(5) needs fib(4) and fib(3); fib(4) needs fib(3) again - the same fib(3) is recomputed many times.
Naive recursion explodes to O(2^n); DP stores each fib(k) once, dropping the time to O(n).
Difference from divide and conquer: D&C is for INDEPENDENT subproblems solved separately (merge sort's halves never repeat); DP is for OVERLAPPING subproblems solved once and shared.
Merge sort has no overlap, so DP would not help it; Fibonacci is almost all overlap, so D&C-style recursion is disastrous there.
Two implementation styles: memoization (top-down recursion plus a cache) and tabulation (bottom-up table).
Decision rule: overlap means DP, independent means divide and conquer.
tags: SURE MARK (May 2019, Oct 2021, Feb 2025, Oct 2025 H)

questions.q: Differentiate memoization and tabulation.
a: Both implement dynamic programming; they differ in direction and in which subproblems get computed.
Memoization is top-down: write the natural recursion, but cache every result so a repeated call returns the stored answer.
Pseudocode: if n in memo: return memo[n]; memo[n] = solve(n-1) + solve(n-2);
return memo[n]
Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table iteratively from the smallest subproblem upward, with no recursion at all.
Pseudocode: table[0] = 0; table[1] = 1; for i in 2..n: table[i] = table[i-1]
+ table[i-2]
Memoization computes only the subproblems actually needed and keeps the recursive structure; tabulation computes everything in order and avoids recursion overhead and stack limits.
Both give O(n) time and O(n) space for Fibonacci.
Memoization is lazier and more intuitive; tabulation is iterative and stack-safe - same DP idea, two flavours.

questions.q: What are the two properties a problem needs for DP?
a: A problem suits dynamic programming only if it has two properties.
Overlapping subproblems: the same smaller problems appear again and again during recursion, so storing answers saves real work.
Without overlap there is nothing to reuse, and plain divide and conquer is the right tool instead.
Optimal substructure: an optimal answer to the whole problem can be constructed from optimal answers to its subproblems.
Without it, combining subproblem answers may not give the global optimum, and DP would produce wrong results.
Example with both: shortest path - the shortest S-to-T path through X combines the shortest S-to-X and X-to-T paths, and subpaths repeat across queries.
Counter-example: merge sort's halves are distinct every time, so it has no overlap and DP adds nothing.
Check both properties before reaching for DP; missing either one means a different technique fits better.

topics.title: Floyd Warshall Algorithm
points: Floyd Warshall finds shortest paths between ALL pairs of vertices: all-pairs shortest path.
It computes the shortest path between EVERY pair of vertices in one run.
DP idea: D[k][i][j] = shortest i-to-j path using only vertices 1..k as intermediates.
Recurrence: D[k][i][j] = min(D[k-1][i][j], D[k-1][i][k] + D[k-1][k][j]).
Meaning: the best i-to-j path either ignores vertex k entirely, or goes i -> ... -> k -> ... -> j.
Base: D[0] holds direct edge weights, 0 on the diagonal, infinity where no edge exists.
Pseudocode: initialise D with edge weights; for k in 1..V: for i in 1..V: for j in 1..V: D[i][j] = min(D[i][j], D[i][k] + D[k][j]).
Only two layers are needed in practice, so the space is O(V^2).
O(V^3) time; handles negative weights but not negative cycles.
Time is O(V^3) from the three nested loops, the price of computing all pairs. It handles negative edge weights correctly, but not negative cycles, where distances would keep shrinking forever.

Trace on a small graph: 1->2 weight 3, 2->3 weight 2, 1->3 weight 10. Initial D[0]: row1 [0, 3, 10], row2 [inf, 0, 2], row3 [inf, inf, 0]. k = 1: allow vertex 1 as an intermediate; no pair improves, since nothing useful routes through vertex 1 yet. k = 2: allow vertex 2; check D[1][3]: min(10, D[1][1][2] + D[1][2][3]) = min(10, 3 + 2) = 5. The path 1->2->3 beats the direct edge. k = 3: allow vertex 3; no further improvement is possible. Final distances: 1->2 = 3, 2->3 = 2, 1->3 = 5 via vertex 2.
Each k either ignores the new vertex or routes through it; that binary choice is the whole recurrence in action. The trace shows the DP table improving exactly when a useful intermediate appears.

Floyd Warshall vs Dijkstra: scope: Floyd Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths in one run; Dijkstra solves single-source, so it must be run V times for all pairs. Weights: Floyd Warshall tolerates negative edge weights; Dijkstra requires non-negative weights. Time: Floyd Warshall is O(V^3); one Dijkstra is O(E log V), so V runs cost O(V * E log V). On dense graphs, V runs of Dijkstra approach O(V^3 log V), making Floyd Warshall competitive or better.

Code simplicity: Floyd Warshall is three nested loops; Dijkstra needs a priority queue plus settled/relaxation bookkeeping. Memory: Floyd Warshall keeps a V x V table, O(V^2); Dijkstra keeps O(V) distances per run.

Rule of thumb: all pairs on a dense graph, or any negative edges, choose Floyd Warshall; single source with non-negative weights, choose Dijkstra. They answer different questions, so the exam tests whether you match the algorithm to the problem.

questions.q: Explain the Floyd Warshall algorithm with its recurrence.
a: Floyd Warshall computes the shortest path between EVERY pair of vertices: the all-pairs shortest path problem.
DP idea: let D[k][i][j] be the shortest distance from i to j using only vertices 1..k as intermediate stops.
Recurrence: D[k][i][j] = min(D[k-1][i][j], D[k-1][i][k] + D[k-1][k][j]).
Meaning: the best i-to-j path either ignores vertex k entirely, or goes i -> ... -> k -> ... -> j.
Base: D[0] holds direct edge weights, 0 on the diagonal, infinity where no edge exists.
Pseudocode:
initialise D with edge weights
for k in 1..V:
for i in 1..V:
for j in 1..V:
D[i][j] = min(D[i][j], D[i][k] + D[k][j])
Only two layers are needed in practice, so the space is O(V^2).
Time is O(V^3) from the three nested loops - the price of computing all pairs.
It handles negative edge weights correctly, but not negative cycles, where distances would keep shrinking forever.
Three loops and one recurrence solve all-pairs shortest paths - the simplest O(V^3) algorithm in the syllabus.

questions.q: Trace Floyd Warshall on a small graph.
a: Graph: 1->2 weight 3, 2->3 weight 2, 1->3 weight 10.
Initial D[0]: row1 [0, 3, 10], row2 [inf, 0, 2], row3 [inf, inf, 0]. k = 1: allow vertex 1 as an intermediate.
No pair improves, since nothing useful routes through vertex 1 yet. k = 2: allow vertex 2.
The path 1->2->3 beats the direct edge. k = 3: allow vertex 3.
No further improvement is possible.
Final distances: 1->2 = 3, 2->3 = 2, 1->3 = 5 via vertex 2.
Each k either ignores the new vertex or routes through it - that binary choice is the whole recurrence in action.
The trace shows the DP table improving exactly when a useful intermediate appears.

questions.q: Compare Floyd Warshall with Dijkstra.
a: Scope: Floyd Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths in one run; Dijkstra solves single-source, so it must be run V times for all pairs.
Weights: Floyd Warshall tolerates negative edge weights; Dijkstra requires non-negative weights.
Time: Floyd Warshall is O(V^3); one Dijkstra is O(E log V), so V runs cost O(V * E log V).
On dense graphs, V runs of Dijkstra approach O(V^3 log V), making Floyd Warshall competitive or better.
Code simplicity: Floyd Warshall is three nested loops; Dijkstra needs a priority queue plus settled/relaxation bookkeeping.
Memory: Floyd Warshall keeps a V x V table, O(V^2); Dijkstra keeps O(V) distances per run.
Rule of thumb: all pairs on a dense graph, or any negative edges - Floyd Warshall; single source with non-negative weights - Dijkstra.
They answer different questions, so the exam tests whether you match the algorithm to the problem.

topics.title: Breadth First Search (BFS)
points: BFS explores a graph level by level using a QUEUE: visit neighbours before going deeper.
Start at source, mark visited, enqueue; dequeue a vertex, enqueue its unvisited neighbours.
Time O(V + E); gives shortest path (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs.

questions.q: Explain BFS with an example. What is its complexity?
a: Breadth First Search explores a graph level by level: all neighbours of the source first, then neighbours of neighbours, using a QUEUE.
Pseudocode:
queue = [source]; visited[source] = True
while queue:
u = queue.pop(0)
for v in neighbours(u):
if not visited[v]: visited[v] = True; queue.append(v)
Trace: S connected to A and B; A connected to C.
Queue starts [S].
Pop S, enqueue A, B -> queue [A, B]. Pop A, enqueue C -> [B, C]. Pop B ->
Visit order: S, A, B, C - level 0, then level 1, then level 2.
Complexity: each vertex is enqueued once and each edge examined once, giving O(V + E) with an adjacency list.
The queue is the key: first-in-first-out order is what enforces the level-by-level discipline.
BFS is the natural way to explore outward evenly, which is why it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

questions.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in unweighted graphs?
a: In an unweighted graph, the shortest path means the fewest edges.
The queue processes vertices strictly in order of their distance from the source: all distance-1 vertices before any distance-2 vertex, and so on.
Therefore the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has arrived via the smallest possible number of edges - no shorter route can exist.
Recording each vertex's parent at discovery time traces one such shortest path back to the source.
With weighted edges this breaks down, because a two-edge path can be shorter than a one-edge path; Dijkstra is needed there.
FIFO order plus unit weights equals shortest paths - remove either ingredient and the guarantee vanishes.

questions.q: What are the applications of BFS?
a: Shortest path in unweighted graphs: fewest hops between two nodes, e.g. degrees of separation in a social network.
Connected components: one BFS from each unvisited vertex labels every component of the graph.
Bipartiteness test: colour levels alternately; an edge joining two same-colour vertices proves the graph is not bipartite.
Web crawlers: expand outward from seed pages level by level, which is BFS over the link graph.
Shortest path in mazes and grids: each step costs one, so BFS finds the quickest route.
Peer-to-peer and broadcast networks use BFS-like flooding to reach all nodes evenly.
Whenever fewest steps or level order matters, BFS is the tool.

topics.title: Depth First Search (DFS)
points: DFS goes as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a STACK or recursion.
Visit a vertex, recursively visit each unvisited neighbour.
Time O(V + E); uses discovery and finish times, useful for cycle detection and topological sort.

questions.q: Explain DFS with an example. What is its complexity?
a: Depth First Search explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion as an implicit stack.
Pseudocode:
dfs(u):
visited[u] = True
for v in neighbours(u):
if not visited[v]: dfs(v)
Trace: edges S-A, S-B, A-C, starting at S.
Visit S; first neighbour A: visit A; A's neighbour C: visit C. C has no
unvisited neighbours: backtrack to A, then to S.
Next neighbour B: visit B. Done. Visit order: S, A, C, B.
Complexity: each vertex is visited once and each edge examined once, giving O(V + E) with an adjacency list.
The recursion stack records the current path, which is why DFS is natural for backtracking-style problems.
DFS trades BFS's level order for depth, which unlocks cycle detection and topological sorting.

questions.q: Compare BFS and DFS.
a: Data structure: BFS uses a queue (FIFO); DFS uses a stack or recursion (LIFO).
Order: BFS visits level by level outward; DFS dives deep down one branch before backtracking.
Shortest paths: BFS finds fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs; DFS gives no such guarantee.
Memory: BFS stores a whole frontier level, O(V) in the worst case; DFS stores one path, O(depth), usually smaller.
Applications: BFS for shortest paths, components and bipartiteness; DFS for cycle detection, topological sort and backtracking search.
Both run in O(V + E) on adjacency lists and visit every reachable vertex exactly once.
Same complexity, opposite exploration order - the exam loves this contrast.

questions.q: What are discovery and finish times in DFS?
a: DFS stamps every vertex twice: discovery time when it is first visited, finish time when all its neighbours are done.
Colour view: white means undiscovered, gray means discovered but still on the recursion stack, black means finished.
Discovery time marks entry, when the vertex turns gray; finish time marks exit, when it turns black.
The intervals nest properly: if v is discovered while u is gray, v's interval sits inside u's, proving v is a descendant of u in the DFS tree.
These times classify edges in directed graphs: a back edge to a gray ancestor reveals a cycle.
Sorting vertices by decreasing finish time yields a topological order of a DAG.
The two timestamps turn a simple walk into a full structural analysis of the graph.

topics.title: Connected Components
points: A connected component is a maximal set of vertices all reachable from each other.
Count components: run DFS or BFS from every unvisited vertex; each launch is one component.
A graph is connected if it has exactly one component.

questions.q: How do you find connected components of a graph?
a: A connected component is a maximal group of vertices all reachable from each other; maximal means no vertex can be added to it.
Algorithm: keep a visited array and a counter starting at 0.
for each vertex v:
if not visited[v]:
run BFS or DFS from v # marks exactly its component
count += 1
Each launch explores precisely one component, because the search cannot cross over to unreachable vertices.
When the loop ends, count equals the number of components and every vertex is labelled with its component.
Complexity is O(V + E), since each vertex and edge is processed once across all launches.
Counting launches of a graph search is the standard components algorithm.

questions.q: How do you test whether a graph is connected?
a: A graph is connected if it has exactly one component, i.e. every vertex is reachable from every other vertex.
Run a single BFS or DFS from any vertex, say vertex 0, and count how many vertices get visited.
If the count equals V, all vertices were reached and the graph is connected.
If fewer than V were visited, some vertices are unreachable and the graph is disconnected.
This is the components algorithm stopped after the first launch, still costing O(V + E).
One search, one count, one answer.

topics.title: DFS of a Directed Graph
points: In directed graphs DFS classifies edges: tree, back, forward, cross.
Tree edge: points to a white (undiscovered) vertex; it becomes part of the DFS tree.
Back edge: points to a gray vertex, i.e. an ancestor on the current recursion stack. Its presence proves a directed cycle exists.
Forward edge: points to a black descendant, skipping down levels of the DFS tree.
Cross edge: points to a black vertex that is neither ancestor nor descendant, typically sitting in another branch or tree.
Edges are classified by the state of the target vertex at the moment it is explored. In undirected graphs only tree and back edges exist, which is why cycle detection there is simpler.
Back edge (to an ancestor) means the directed graph HAS a cycle.
Cycle detection method: a directed graph has a cycle if and only if DFS encounters a back edge, an edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack.
Colour scheme: white means unvisited, gray means on the current DFS path, black means fully explored.
Pseudocode: dfs(u): colour[u] = gray; for v in neighbours(u): if colour[v] == gray: cycle found, return True; if colour[v] == white and dfs(v): return True; colour[u] = black; return False.

Trace: edges A->B, B->C, C->A. dfs(A) grays A; dfs(B) grays B; dfs(C) sees neighbour A which is gray, a back edge, so the cycle is confirmed. Without the gray distinction, the edge C->A would look like an ordinary visited edge and the cycle would be missed.
Complexity is O(V + E). For undirected graphs the rule simplifies: a visited neighbour that is not the parent means a cycle.
Finishing times in decreasing order give a topological sort of a DAG.

Topological ordering of a DAG lists vertices so that every directed edge u->v has u before v; it models task scheduling with prerequisites. It exists only for directed acyclic graphs, since a cycle makes ordering impossible (each vertex would have to precede itself).
DFS method: run DFS over the whole graph; whenever a vertex finishes (turns black), push it onto a stack. After DFS completes, pop the stack: vertices emerge in decreasing order of finish time.
Why it works: for any edge u->v, v finishes before u (v is explored from u), so u is pushed later and popped earlier.
Example: edges A->B, A->C, B->D, C->D. Valid orders include A, B, C, D and A, C, B, D. Complexity is O(V + E).

topics.title: Backtracking: Concept
points: Backtracking builds candidates step by step and abandons a path as soon as it cannot lead to a solution.

Backtracking solves constraint problems by building candidates one choice at a time, abandoning a partial candidate the moment it cannot lead to a valid answer. Think of a maze: walk forward; at a dead end, walk back to the last junction and try another turn; the walking back is the backtrack.
It explores a state space tree; a bounding function prunes hopeless branches.

The state space tree is the tree of all partial candidates: the root is the empty answer, and each child adds one more choice. A complete root-to-leaf path is one full candidate; internal nodes are the prefixes tried along the way.

Pruning means cutting off a subtree without exploring it, using a bounding function that proves no solution lies inside. Good pruning is what separates backtracking from blind brute force; it can shrink an exponential search to something practical. The tree organises the search; pruning keeps it affordable.
A node is promising if a solution might still lie below it; else backtrack to the parent.

A node is called promising if the partial answer could still extend to a solution; only promising nodes are expanded. Example: in sum of subsets with target 5, any branch whose partial sum already exceeds 5 is pruned immediately.
Examples: N-Queens, sum of subsets, Hamiltonian circuit, graph colouring.
N-Queens example: queens are placed row by row; the moment a queen is attacked, that placement is undone and the next column is tried.
Pseudocode shape: solve(partial): if partial is complete: record it and return; for each legal next choice: extend partial; solve(partial); undo the extension (the backtrack).
Backtracking is organised trial and error: try, test early, undo fast.

Backtracking vs brute force: brute force generates every complete candidate first and only then tests whether it satisfies the constraints. Backtracking tests partial candidates during construction and abandons a branch as soon as it is doomed.

Example: 4-queens by brute force would test all 4^4 = 256 full placements; backtracking kills most branches after one or two rows. Both are exponential in the worst case, since a problem may genuinely need the whole tree explored, but in practice backtracking with strong pruning runs far faster, because dead branches die young.

Memory also favours backtracking: it needs only the current path, O(depth), while brute force may hold many candidates. Brute force checks everything at the end; backtracking checks early and quits early.

topics.title: N-Queens Problem
points: Place N queens on an N x N board so no two attack each other: different rows, columns and diagonals.
The N-Queens problem asks for placements of N queens on an N x N board so that no two queens attack each other. Attack rule: no two queens may share a row, a column, or a diagonal.
Place queens row by row; for each row try columns left to right, skipping attacked squares.
Backtracking strategy: place queens row by row from top to bottom, so rows are automatically distinct.
Pseudocode: place(row): if row == N: record the board and return; for col in 0..N-1: if square (row, col) is safe: put queen; place(row+1); remove queen (the backtrack).
Safety test against earlier queens at (r, c): col != c for the column, and abs(row - r) != abs(col - c) for the diagonals.
If no column works, backtrack: move the previous queen to its next column.
If no column is safe in a row, the recursion returns and the previous queen moves to its next column; that is the backtrack step.

How to test whether a square is under attack: since queens are placed top to bottom, only earlier rows can threaten the new square. Column test: the new square's column must differ from every earlier queen's column. Diagonal test: for each earlier queen at (r, c), the new square (row, col) is attacked if abs(row - r) == abs(col - c).

The absolute-difference trick works because diagonals have slope 1: equal row-gap and column-gap means the same diagonal. If the column test and both diagonal directions pass, the square is safe to use.
Example: queens at (0,1) and (1,3); square (2,0): columns differ; |2-0|=2 vs |0-1|=1 fine; |2-1|=1 vs |0-3|=3 fine, so it is safe. Three cheap arithmetic tests replace any board scanning.

State space tree for 4-queens: level 0 is the root, the empty board; each deeper level adds one queen in the next row. Level 1 has 4 children: the first-row queen in columns 1, 2, 3, 4. Level 2: under each level-1 node, only columns not attacked by the first queen become children, so most branches are already pruned.

For example, a queen at (1,1) attacks column 1 and the diagonal through column 2 of row 2, leaving few children. Levels 3 and 4 continue the same way; branches die whenever a row has no safe column, triggering a backtrack. Only the paths that place all 4 queens safely reach level 4: exactly 2 leaves, which are the 2 solutions. The tree visualises pruning: the vast majority of the 4^4 theoretical nodes never get created.
Results: 4-queens has 2 solutions and 8-queens has 92; the worst case is exponential but pruning makes it practical.
One queen per row plus the attack test turns an impossible search into a guided one.

topics.title: Sum of Subsets Problem
points: Given n numbers and target sum m, find all subsets whose elements add to m.
Problem: given n numbers (weights) and a target m, find all subsets whose elements sum to exactly m.
Build subsets element by element (include or skip); prune when partial sum exceeds m.
Sort the numbers first; bounding uses remaining sum to prune hopeless branches.
Sort the weights first, then decide for each weight in order: include it or skip it.

Pseudocode with pruning: backtrack(k, cur, rem), where k = next index, cur = sum so far, rem = sum of weights k..n. If cur == m: record the subset and return. If k > n or cur > m: return (overshoot, prune). If cur + rem < m: return (cannot reach m, prune). Otherwise backtrack(k+1, cur + w[k], rem - w[k]) to include w[k], and backtrack(k+1, cur, rem - w[k]) to skip it.
Trace: weights [2, 3, 5], target 5. Include 2, include 3: cur = 5, record {2,3}. Backtrack, skip 3: cur = 2; include 5 gives cur = 7 > 5, prune. The remaining branches yield {5}.
The two bounding tests, overshoot and cannot-reach, kill dead branches early.

Bounding functions prove a branch is hopeless so it can be pruned without exploration. Upper bound (overshoot): if the current partial sum already exceeds m, no extension can fix it, so prune the branch. Lower bound (unreachable): if the current sum plus the sum of ALL remaining weights is still below m, the target is unreachable, so prune.

In the fixed-tuple formulation these become precise tests at each node k: include w[k+1] only if cur + w[k+1] <= m (fits without overshoot); skip w[k+1] only if cur + remaining - w[k+1] >= m (target still reachable). Both bounds need the weights sorted and the remaining sums precomputed.
One bound cuts branches that are too big, the other cuts branches that are too small.

Time complexity: in the worst case the algorithm explores the include-or-skip choice for every weight, 2^n subsets, so O(2^n) time. Pruning with sorted weights and the two bounding functions cuts typical searches dramatically, but the worst case stands.
The problem is NP-complete: no known algorithm solves all instances in polynomial time. Space is O(n) for the recursion stack plus the current subset; the tree itself is never stored.
This exponential nature is exactly why backtracking with pruning, rather than brute force, is taught for this problem.

questions.q: Explain the sum of subsets problem with backtracking.
a: Problem: given n numbers (weights) and a target m, find all subsets whose elements sum to exactly m.
Sort the weights first; then decide for each weight in order: include it or skip it.
Pseudocode with pruning:
backtrack(k, cur, rem): # k = next index, cur = sum so far, rem = sum of
weights k..n
if cur == m: record the subset; return
if k > n or cur > m: return # overshoot: prune
if cur + rem < m: return # cannot reach m: prune
backtrack(k+1, cur + w[k], rem - w[k]) # include w[k]
backtrack(k+1, cur, rem - w[k]) # skip w[k]
Trace: weights [2, 3, 5], target 5.

topics.title: Hamiltonian Circuit Problem
points: A Hamiltonian circuit visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start.
A Hamiltonian circuit is a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start vertex.
Backtracking: build a path vertex by vertex; next vertex must be adjacent and unvisited.
Backtracking builds the path vertex by vertex; each new vertex must be adjacent to the last one and not visited before.

Pseudocode: path = [start]; extend(): if len(path) == n: if edge from path[-1] to start exists: circuit found; return; for each neighbour v of path[-1]: if v not in path: append v; extend(); remove v (the backtrack).
Trace on square A-B-C-D-A: path grows A -> B -> C -> D; D connects back to A, so A-B-C-D-A is a Hamiltonian circuit.
If stuck before covering all vertices, backtrack; a full path that connects back to start is the answer.
If a dead end is hit (no unvisited neighbour and the path is incomplete), the last vertex is removed and the next neighbour is tried.
Worst case is O(n!) but adjacency pruning, only real neighbours are ever tried, keeps small graphs practical. The problem is NP-complete, so exponential search is expected rather than a flaw.
Grow the path, demand adjacency, backtrack on dead ends, close the cycle at the end.

Hamiltonian vs Euler circuit: a Hamiltonian circuit visits every VERTEX exactly once, then returns to the start; edges may be skipped. An Euler circuit uses every EDGE exactly once and returns to the start; vertices may repeat.
Euler has a simple test: a connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree. Hamiltonian has no such easy test; it is NP-complete and needs backtracking search.

Example: the square A-B-C-D-A is both Hamiltonian (visits A, B, C, D) and Eulerian (uses all 4 edges; every degree is 2). Add a diagonal A-C: degrees become A:3, C:3, odd, so no Euler circuit exists; but A-B-C-D-A remains Hamiltonian. Euler cares about edges and has a degree test; Hamilton cares about vertices and has no shortcut.

Pruning in the search: only neighbours of the current last vertex are ever tried, so non-adjacent vertices are pruned by construction; vertices already in the path are skipped, which enforces the exactly-once rule automatically; if the unvisited vertices cannot form a connected chain back to the start, the branch is abandoned early; fixing the start vertex avoids rediscovering the same circuit n times in rotated form; a degree check helps, since a vertex (other than the start) with fewer than 2 unused incident edges can never belong to a circuit.

Despite all this, the worst case stays exponential: pruning shrinks the constant, not the complexity class. Adjacency plus visited-set plus start-fixing is the standard pruning package for this problem.

topics.title: History and Application Areas of Python
points: Python was created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991.

Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer, started the project in the late 1980s and released the first version, Python 0.9.0, in 1991. Python 2.0 (2000) and Python 3.0 (2008) made it a major modern language, and today it is one of the most popular languages in the world.
It is named after the comedy show Monty Python, not the snake.

Van Rossum led the language for many years as its 'Benevolent Dictator For Life' (BDFL) until 2018. Because Python was free and open source, thousands of developers around the world contributed to it.
Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language.

Key features: simple and easy to learn (syntax reads almost like plain English); interpreted (code runs line by line without a separate compilation step, so testing and debugging is fast); free and open source; portable (the same program runs on Windows, Linux and Mac with little or no change); a huge standard library (ready-made modules for files, maths, dates, web work); dynamically typed (you never declare variable types, Python decides at run time, e.g. x = 10 and type(x) needs no declaration).

Why interpreted: source code is first converted into an intermediate form called bytecode, then the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) reads the bytecode and executes it line by line. A compiled language like C must first be fully translated into machine code by a compiler before it can run.
You can type commands one by one in the interactive shell (the >>> prompt) and see each result at once, so you can run, fix an error and run again immediately with no waiting for compilation.

Ways to run Python: interactive mode (type python3 in the terminal, one line at a time, best for quick experiments); script mode (write code in a .py file and run python3 file.py, the normal way); IDEs and editors (VS Code, PyCharm, IDLE, with debugging and code completion); Jupyter notebooks (code runs in cells with output below each cell, popular in data science); online interpreters (websites running Python in the browser with nothing installed). For exams, remember interactive mode and script mode as the two basic ways.
Python source files use the .py extension, for example program.py. Related extensions: .pyc for compiled bytecode files that Python creates automatically, and .pyw for windowed scripts on Windows.
It is free and open source with a huge collection of ready-made libraries. A large community and libraries like Numpy and Django mean almost every problem already has a Python solution.
Used in web development, data science, AI and machine learning, automation and game development.

Application areas: web development (Django and Flask build sites and web apps, handling pages, users and databases); data science and AI (Numpy, Pandas and scikit-learn for data analysis and machine learning); automation and scripting (short scripts for repetitive tasks like renaming files, sending emails, scraping pages); education and research (simple syntax makes it the first language taught in many schools, widely used by scientists); game development (Pygame for simple 2D games); desktop applications (Tkinter and PyQt for GUI apps); cybersecurity (security tools, scanners, penetration-testing scripts).
Remember three facts for full marks: creator = Guido van Rossum, year = 1991, name from = the Monty Python show.

a: Python is simple and easy to learn: its syntax reads almost like plain English, so beginners write working programs quickly.

A large community and libraries like Numpy and Django mean almost every problem already has a Python solution.
These features are why Python is the first choice for beginners and for fields like data science and AI.

questions.q: Explain the application areas of Python.
a: Python is a general-purpose language, so it is used in many different fields.
Web development: sites and web apps are built with frameworks like Django and Flask, which handle pages, users and databases quickly.
Data science and AI: Numpy, Pandas and scikit-learn are used for data analysis and machine learning models.

Desktop applications: tools like Tkinter and PyQt create GUI apps that run on the computer.
Cybersecurity: Python is used to write security tools, scanners and penetration-testing scripts.
So from websites to robots, Python fits almost everywhere, which is why companies everywhere hire Python developers.

a: An interpreted language is one whose code is run line by line by a program called an interpreter, without a separate compilation step.
A compiled language like C must first be fully translated into machine code by a compiler before it can run.
In Python, the source code is first converted into an intermediate form called bytecode.
Then the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) reads the bytecode and executes it line by line.
You can even type commands one by one in the interactive shell (the >>> prompt) and see each result at once.
This means you can run a program, see an error, fix it and run again immediately, with no waiting for compilation.
That is why testing and development in Python is fast and beginner friendly.
So Python is called an interpreted language because its code is executed by an interpreter (the PVM) instead of being compiled to machine code first.

questions.q: What are the different ways to run Python?
a: Interactive mode: type python3 in the terminal and run one line at a time; best for quick experiments.
Script mode: write code in a .py file and run it with python3 file.py; the normal way to run full programs.
IDEs and editors: tools like VS Code, PyCharm or IDLE run Python with debugging and code completion.
Jupyter notebooks: code runs in cells with output shown below each cell; popular in data science.
Online interpreters: websites that run Python in the browser with nothing installed.
For exams, remember interactive mode and script mode as the two basic ways of running Python.

questions.q: What is the extension of a Python file?
a: Python source files use the .py extension, for example program.py.
The .py extension tells the operating system and the interpreter that the file holds Python code.
Related extensions: .pyc for compiled bytecode files that Python creates automatically, and .pyw for windowed scripts on Windows.
In answers and file handling questions, always name Python files with the .py extension.

questions.q: Who developed Python and when was it released?
a: Python was developed by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer.
He started the project in the late 1980s and released the first version, Python 0.9.0, in 1991.
Python was named after the British comedy show Monty Python, not the snake.
Van Rossum led the language for many years as its "Benevolent Dictator For Life" (BDFL) until 2018.
Because Python was free and open source, thousands of developers around the world contributed to it.
The release of Python 2.0 (2000) and Python 3.0 (2008) made it a major modern language.
Today Python is one of the most popular languages in the world.
Remember three facts for full marks: creator = Guido van Rossum, year = 1991, name from = the Monty Python show.

topics.title: Structure of a Program, Identifiers and Keywords
points: A Python program is a set of statements executed one after another from top to bottom.
No semicolons or curly braces are needed; indentation (spaces) defines blocks of code.
An identifier is a name for variables, functions or classes; it must start with a letter or underscore.
Keywords are reserved words like if, for, while, def, class and import; they cannot be used as names.
Python is case sensitive: Name and name are two different identifiers.

questions.q: What is an identifier? State the rules for naming identifiers.
a: An identifier is a name given to program elements like variables, functions, classes and modules.
Example: in total = 10, the name total is an identifier.
Rule 1: it can contain letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9) and underscores (_).
Rule 2: it must start with a letter or an underscore, never with a digit, so _name and name1 are valid but 1name is not.
Rule 3: it cannot be a keyword like if, for, while or class, because those have fixed meanings in the language.
Rule 4: Python is case sensitive, so Name and name are two different identifiers.
Rule 5: no spaces or special symbols like @, - or $ are allowed in a name.
Good practice: use meaningful names like total_marks instead of single letters like x, so the code is easy to read.

questions.q: What are keywords? Give any five examples.
a: Keywords are reserved words in Python that have a fixed meaning and purpose.
They are part of the language itself, so you cannot use them as variable or function names.
Five examples: if (decision making), else (alternative branch), for (looping), while (condition loop) and def (defining a function).
More examples: return, import, class, True, False and None.
If you try to write name = if, Python gives a syntax error because if is reserved.
There are about 35 keywords in Python 3, and the list is fixed for the language.
You can see all of them by running help("keywords") in the Python shell.
In short: keywords belong to Python, so programmers must pick other names for their own variables.

questions.q: Explain the structure of a Python program.
a: A Python program is a set of statements executed one after another from top to bottom.
A statement is a single instruction, like x = 10.
Related statements are grouped into a block using the same indentation (spaces at the start of the line).
Python needs no semicolons to end lines and no curly braces for blocks, unlike C or Java.
A typical program has: comments, import statements, variable assignments, function definitions and the main logic.
Example code:
if x > 5:
print("big")
Here the print statement is inside the if block because it is indented one level deeper.
If the indentation is wrong, Python gives an IndentationError, so neat spacing is part of the structure.

questions.q: Demonstrate the significance of indentation in Python programming.
a: In most languages braces mark a block of code; in Python, indentation (spaces at the line start) does that job.
